title: How Ripple is checked
text:
# How Ripple is checked

Four groups of checks, each with a threshold set before the fit, and each able to
fail in public. They are written to `trust.json` and rendered as cards on the home
page and on `/method`.

## 1. Convergence — did the sampler do its job?

| Check | Threshold | Why this number |
|---|---|---|
| R-hat | ≤ 1.01 | Independent chains must agree. Above 1.01 they found different answers. |
| Effective sample size | ≥ 400 | Below this the interval edges move when you refit, so the 90% interval is not stable. |
| Divergences | 0 | A divergence means the sampler could not explore part of the posterior, so the tails are understated. |

## 2. Fit — does it describe the data it was given?

**Posterior predictive coverage ≥ 85%.** Simulate new weeks from the fitted model and
check how often the real week falls inside its own 90% range. Far below 90% means
overconfidence; far above means the intervals are padded.

## 3. Parameter recovery — does it find effects that are really there?

Demo only. The synthetic company was generated from known parameter values, so we can
ask the question that matters: **does the 94% interval contain the truth?** 30 of 30
planted values are recovered, including every segment elasticity, every promo lift, the
post-promo dip, the trait coefficients and the overdispersion.

This is the check that cannot be run on real data, and it is the reason the demo company
is synthetic rather than scraped.

## 4. Time holdout — does it predict weeks it has never seen?

The last 12 weeks are removed, the model is **refitted** from scratch on the rest, and
then asked to predict the hidden weeks.

- **Coverage of the 90% interval:** 92%.
- **Error vs. a naive baseline:** 18.4% MAPE against 44.7% for a same-week-last-year
  guess.

Beating a naive baseline is a low bar. That is exactly why failing it would matter.

## 5. Is the launch tracker's updating honest?

A separate question, answered separately — see `limits.md` and the calibration chart on
`/method`. Simulation-based calibration generates launches whose truth is drawn from the
same prior the update uses, so a 90% interval **must** cover the truth 90% of the time
if the computation is right. The stress arm breaks an assumption on purpose and shows
coverage dropping, because knowing where a method fails is part of trusting it.

title: Limits — where Ripple is wrong, and how you would know
text:
# Limits — where Ripple is wrong, and how you would know

## The launch tracker is an approximation, with a gate

After a launch, Ripple updates the forecast with Bayes' rule: the fitted model is the
prior, the new weeks are the likelihood, importance weighting gives the posterior. The
other parameters stay at their posterior draws; only the one unknown is re-learned.

This is exact Bayes for the joint model **as long as the importance weights behave**.
When the launch weeks are very surprising, a handful of samples carry all the weight and
the answer becomes noise. So Ripple measures that directly:

- **Pareto k-hat > 0.7** (server) or **weight ESS < 300** (browser) → the badge flips to
  **"Refit needed"**, and the full model is refitted with the new rows.

The limit it cannot fix on its own: the existing parameters are *not* re-learned from the
launch weeks. The refit path does that.

## "Lift" is observed vs. counterfactual, not automatically causal

The lift Ripple reports is the observed outcome against what the model predicted with no
change, for the same cells and weeks. That is causal only if:

1. no other change happened in the same weeks;
2. untreated cities and groups were not affected;
3. the demand pattern was stable.

The `/launch` page shows these three as a checklist rather than hiding them, because the
model cannot verify any of them.

**The fix is in your hands:** keep a random holdout group — for example 10% of users get
no offer. If the CSV has a `holdout` column, Ripple uses those cells as the control and
labels the result **"Experiment"** instead of **"Model-based estimate"**. The gift-boxes
demo launch has one, so you can see both labels.

## The known failure mode: a launch that ramps up

The model has no ramp-up term. A launch that builds slowly over its first weeks looks
like a *weak* launch to Ripple, and the calibration study measures exactly how bad that
gets: coverage of the 90% interval falls well below 90% in the stress arm. It is on the
`/method` page next to the arms that pass, on purpose.

## Extrapolation

A new city is a forecast from its traits. When a standardized trait falls outside the
training range, Ripple raises an extrapolation flag, names the trait, and says the
interval is a **lower bound** on the real uncertainty. Miami in the demo is out of range
on income and age — it is there to show the warning, not to be a good recommendation.

## No competitor reaction

The model answers what happens if you change your price. It does not model what a
competitor does next. The Nimble market scan in "Ask Ripple" shows competitor prices and
current offers with sources as **context**, clearly labelled as web data, and it is never
an input to the model.

## Numbers and the language model

The language model never produces a number. Every number in an answer comes from a tool
result — the posterior, or a cited web result labelled as web — and a number guard
rejects any answer containing a figure that no tool returned. If the guard trips, the
template answer is shown instead.

## The demo data is synthetic

"Brightside Coffee Subscriptions" is fictional, with a fixed seed and planted parameter
values. That is a deliberate trade: it makes parameter recovery provable, which no real
dataset allows. City traits are ACS-shaped but illustrative, not pulled live.

title: Model card — Ripple demand model
text:
# Model card — Ripple demand model

## What it does

Ripple answers "what happens to sales if…?" questions — a promotion, a price change,
or a launch in a city with no history — and answers with a **distribution**, not a
number: incremental units, revenue and profit against a no-change baseline, a 90%
interval, and the probability the change pays.

## The model

One row of data is one week × city × customer segment.

```
y[c,s,t] ~ NegativeBinomial(mu, phi)

log mu = log(share[c,s])                 customer mix of the city (a fixed offset)
       + a_city[c]                        how big this city is
       + a_seg[s]                         how much this segment buys per head
       + e[s]      * log(price / base)    price elasticity, per segment
       + b_promo[s] * promo               the deal signal of being on promotion
       + b_feature  * feature             the email campaign flag
       + b_dip      * promo_last_week     pull-forward: last week's promo borrowed from this one
       + season(t)                        2 Fourier pairs, 52-week period

a_city[c] = g0 + X_city[c]·g + tau_city · z_city[c]
e[s] ~ Normal(mu_e, sigma_e),  mu_e ~ Normal(-1.5, 0.5),  sigma_e ~ HalfNormal(0.5)
```

## Why each part

| Part | Why it is there | What breaks without it |
|---|---|---|
| **Negative Binomial** | Weekly unit counts are overdispersed — the variance is much larger than the mean. | Poisson would call normal week-to-week variation a surprise, and every interval would be far too narrow. |
| **log–log price term** | `e[s]` *is* the elasticity: a 1% price rise changes demand by `e[s]`%. | A linear price term gives a number that means nothing at a different price level, and can predict negative demand. |
| **Elasticity per segment, partially pooled** | Students and retirees do not respond to price the same way. Pooling lets a segment with thin data borrow strength from the others. | Pooled: targeted offers look identical for everyone. Unpooled: a small segment's elasticity is driven by noise. |
| **Partially pooled promo lift** | Being on promotion lifts demand beyond the price cut itself — the deal is a signal. | The price term alone understates a promotion, then overstates the discount needed next time. |
| **Post-promo dip (`b_dip`)** | A promotion pulls purchases forward from the following week. | Promotions look better than they are, because the borrowed sales are never paid back in the model. |
| **Hierarchical city effect on traits** | `a_city` is predicted from population, income and age, so a city with **no history at all** still has a forecast — with honest uncertainty from `tau_city`. | New-city questions become unanswerable, which is a third of the product. |
| **Customer-mix offset** | Volume scales with who lives there, so a new city with a different mix is handled without refitting. | A young, student-heavy city gets forecast as if it had the average mix. |
| **Fourier seasonality** | Yearly demand shape, with few enough parameters to extrapolate past the training weeks. | Season is confounded with the promotion calendar, and `b_promo` absorbs it. |

## Fitting

nutpie NUTS, 4 chains × 1000 draws, `target_accept = 0.99`, fixed seed.

`target_accept` is higher than the usual 0.8 on purpose. At the default the fit had
28 divergences out of 4000 draws; `e` and `b_promo` are now non-centred (with only
four segments, sampling them against their own scale makes a funnel) and
`target_accept = 0.99` takes the count to zero.

A customer upload gets 2 chains × 500 draws with a 90-second budget; past the budget
the run falls back to ADVI and is labelled **fast approximation** everywhere it is shown.

## What it is not

- **No competitor reaction.** It answers what happens if *you* change your price, not
  what happens after a competitor answers back. The market scan in "Ask Ripple" shows
  competitor prices as context and is never an input to the model.
- **Effects are assumed stable** across the forecast horizon.
- **A new city is a forecast from its traits.** Outside the training trait range the
  interval is a lower bound on the real uncertainty, and Ripple says so on the chart.
- **The demo company is synthetic.** That is what makes parameter recovery provable;
  on your own data there is no truth to check against, and the holdout does that job.
